decks.title: Arrays in Rows and Columns: Declaration, Input and Display
goals: Declare, create and initialise a double-dimensional array
Find the number of rows, columns and elements, and use valid subscripts
Accept the elements of a table with nested loops
Display a table in matrix format

slides.heading: Double-dimensional arrays
slides.body_md: Part 1: **declaring**, **initialising**, **accepting** and **displaying** a table of values with an array that has **rows and columns**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: rows and columns, declaration, initialiser list, length of rows and columns, input with nested loops, matrix display and subscript errors
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to double dimensional arrays. In this part we declare and create an array with rows and columns, give it values with an initialiser list, find how many rows and columns it has, accept its elements with nested loops, and display them in matrix format. We finish with the error that appears when a subscript is out of range.

slides.heading: Data in rows and columns
slides.body_md: A single-dimensional array is a list. When data forms a **table**, for example the sales of shops on several days, a **double-dimensional array** keeps it in **rows and columns**. An element is named by **two subscripts**: `a[i][j]` is in row `i` and column `j`.

visual.caption: A double-dimensional array is a table: element a[i][j] is in row i and column j.

slides.narration: A single dimensional array holds a list of values. Many problems need a table, such as the sales of three shops over four days. A double dimensional array keeps such a table in rows and columns. Each element has two subscripts. The first one gives the row and the second one gives the column. Both subscripts start from zero, so the first element is in row zero and column zero.

slides.heading: Declaring and creating
slides.body_md:
```java
int[][] m = new int[3][4];
```

Two pairs of brackets mean two dimensions. In **new int[3][4]** the first size is the number of **rows** and the second is the number of **columns**.

rows: m refers to a double-dimensional array of int

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the declaration int[][] m = new int[3][4] has these parts: the type, the creation of 3 rows and 4 columns, the number of rows 3, the number of columns 4 and the value 0 of the last element
visual.caption: The first size is the number of rows; the second size is the number of columns.

slides.narration: The declaration has two pairs of brackets, one for each dimension. In the creation part, the first size is the number of rows and the second size is the number of columns. So this statement makes three rows and four columns, which are twelve elements. The length of the array is the number of rows, the length of the first row is the number of columns, and the last element is in row two and column three.

slides.heading: Default values
slides.body_md: When an array is created, **every element is given a default value**: 0 for int, 0.0 for double, false for boolean and null for String and other objects.

visual.alt: Table of the default values of a new array: int elements are 0, double elements are 0.0, boolean elements are false and String elements are null
visual.caption: No element of a new array is ever undefined.

slides.narration: When a new array is created, Java fills every element with a default value. For int this value is zero, for double it is zero point zero, for boolean it is false, and for String it is null. So a program never meets an undefined element, but a student should still store the real values before using the array.

visual.alt: Table of five expressions on the array fare: fare.length gives 2; fare[0].length gives 3; fare[0][0] gives 12; fare[1][0] gives 10; fare[1][2] gives 20
visual.caption: Subscripts start from 0 in both directions.

slides.narration: Let us find the value of five expressions on the fare array. The length of the array is the number of rows. The length of the first row is the number of columns. Subscripts zero and zero give the first element. Subscripts one and zero give the first element of the second row. The last element is in row one and column two. Remember that the row subscript is always written first.

slides.heading: Rows, columns and elements
slides.body_md: The number of elements is **rows × columns**, and the memory used is that number multiplied by the size of one element (4 bytes for an int).

visual.alt: Table of the size of a table with 5 rows and 6 columns: 5 rows, 6 columns, 30 elements and 120 bytes at 4 bytes for each int

slides.narration: For a table with five rows and six columns, the length of the array gives five and the length of the first row gives six. The number of elements is five times six, which is thirty. An int takes four bytes, so the memory used is one hundred and twenty bytes. The number of elements is always rows multiplied by columns, and not their sum.

slides.heading: Accepting the elements
slides.body_md: Read the order first, create the array, then use **nested loops**: the **outer loop runs over the rows** and the **inner loop over the columns**, so the elements are read **row by row**.

visual.alt: Flow of accepting a table: read r and c, create the array, start the outer loop over the row i, run the inner loop over the column j, read a[i][j] and move to the next row
visual.caption: The array can be created only after r and c are known.

slides.narration: To accept a table, first read the number of rows and columns, and then create the array with those sizes. Then use two loops, one inside the other. The outer loop takes one row at a time. The inner loop takes the columns of that row, and each pass reads one element with the next int method of Scanner. The elements are therefore read row by row.

slides.narration: Here is a complete program. The first two numbers typed, two and four, give two rows and four columns. The next four numbers fill row zero and the last four fill row one. Both loops use the order variables, so the program works for any size. The second pair of loops displays each row on its own line.

slides.heading: Displaying in matrix format
slides.body_md: Print each element **without a line break**, and give **one println after the inner loop** to end the row. Leaving it out, or printing every element with println, spoils the matrix shape.

rows: print for elements, println after each row
println after the inner loop left out

visual.alt: Table of three ways to display a 2 by 2 table: print with println after each row gives 8 9 / 6 7; leaving out the println gives 8 9 6 7; println for every element gives 8 / 9 / 6 / 7
visual.caption: The empty println after the inner loop ends the row.

slides.narration: To display a table in matrix format, print each element with the print method, followed by a space, and end the row with an empty println after the inner loop. The table shows what happens when this is changed. Without the empty println, all the values run together on one line. With println for every element, there is one value on each line.

slides.heading: How the loops visit the elements
slides.body_md: In **row-major order** the row subscript stays fixed while the column subscript goes through all its values. The **column number changes fastest**.

visual.alt: Trace table of the loops over a table with 2 rows and 3 columns: the loop visits row 0 with columns 0 to 2 and then row 1 with columns 0 to 2; the elements are 5, 8, 2, 7, 1, 9
visual.caption: The column number j changes fastest.

slides.narration: The trace table shows the order in which the loops reach the elements of a table with two rows and three columns. The row number stays at zero while the column number goes from zero to two. Then the row number becomes one and the columns are visited again. The column number changes fastest, and this is the order in which input is read.

sections.heading: 1. Rows, columns and declaration
sections.body_md:
A **double-dimensional array** stores values of one data type in **rows and columns**; an element is identified by two subscripts, `a[i][j]` (row, then column), both starting from 0.

```java
int[][] m = new int[3][4];
```

- `new int[3][4]` creates 3 rows and 4 columns, 12 elements: the first size is the rows.
- `m.length` is the number of rows (`3`) and `m[0].length` the number of columns (`4`).
- The number of elements is rows multiplied by columns; the memory is that number multiplied by the size of one element.
- Java stores the table as an array of arrays: `m[1]` is a whole row.

The number, counted from 0, that gives the position of an element in a row or a column.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Rows and columns exchanged in `new int[rows][columns]`.
- `<=` in a loop limit, which goes past the last element.
- The sum variable declared before the outer loop.
- Forgetting `System.out.println();` after the inner loop.
- Using `a[i][i]` on a table that is not square; forgetting that the centre of an odd matrix is counted twice if both diagonal sums are added.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Output questions: each line in the exact order and format; matrix layout kept.
- Error questions: the error named and the reason given.
- Programs (15 marks): class and method structure, input of the order and the elements, nested loops, the logic (sums, diagonal conditions), output, variable description or comments.

cards.front_md: What is a double-dimensional array?
cards.back_md: An array of arrays that stores values of one data type in rows and columns; elements need two subscripts.

cards.front_md: What does new int[3][4] create?
cards.back_md: A table with 3 rows and 4 columns, that is 12 int elements (the first size is the rows).

cards.front_md: Which subscript comes first in a[i][j]?
cards.back_md: The row subscript i, then the column subscript j.

cards.front_md: First element of a double-dimensional array
cards.back_md: a[0][0] (subscripts start from 0).

cards.front_md: Last element of an array with r rows and c columns
How to find the number of rows of array a
cards.back_md: a.length

cards.front_md: How to find the number of columns of array a
cards.back_md: a[0].length (the length of the first row).

cards.front_md: Number of elements of a table
cards.back_md: rows multiplied by columns, for example a.length * a[0].length.

cards.front_md: Why is length written without brackets for an array?
cards.back_md: length is a field, not a method: a.length() gives "cannot find symbol".

cards.front_md: Default values of a new array
cards.back_md: int 0, double 0.0, boolean false, String null.

cards.front_md: What is an initialiser list?
cards.back_md: Values in braces, one inner list for each row, used to create and fill the array in its declaration.

cards.front_md: What does a[1] stand for in a double-dimensional array?
cards.back_md: The whole second row (a single-dimensional array), not one element.

cards.front_md: What is row-major order?
cards.back_md: Visiting the elements row by row; the column subscript changes fastest.

cards.front_md: Which loop is the outer loop when a table is read row by row?
cards.back_md: The loop over the rows; the inner loop is over the columns.

cards.front_md: How is a table accepted from the keyboard?
cards.back_md: `a[i][j] = sc.nextInt();` inside nested loops over the rows and the columns.

cards.front_md: How is a table displayed in matrix format?
cards.back_md: print for each element with a space, and an empty println after the inner loop for the end of each row.

cards.front_md: Output if println is left out after the inner loop
cards.back_md: All the values appear on one line, for example `8 9 6 7`.

cards.front_md: When is ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException thrown?
cards.back_md: When a row or column subscript is negative or not less than the length; for a[3][0] on 3 rows: java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3.

cards.front_md: Which loop condition is safe for rows?
cards.back_md: `i < a.length` (not <=).

cards.front_md: Sum of each row: where is the sum set to 0?
cards.back_md: Inside the outer loop, before the inner loop begins.

cards.front_md: Sum of each row: where is the sum displayed?
cards.back_md: After the inner loop ends, inside the outer loop.

cards.front_md: Sum of each column: which loop is outer?
cards.back_md: The loop over the columns, with the limit a[0].length; the inner loop is over the rows.

cards.front_md: Effect of declaring the sum before the outer loop
cards.back_md: Totals carry over: `33 / 67 / 91` instead of `33 / 34 / 24` for the sales table.

cards.front_md: Sum of all row sums compared with sum of all column sums
cards.back_md: They are equal: both equal the sum of all the elements.

cards.front_md: How can one pair of loops give row and column totals?
cards.back_md: Keep two arrays: rowTot[i] and colTot[j] both receive a[i][j].

cards.front_md: Average of a column of r rows
cards.back_md: sum divided by r, with a cast: (double) cs / a.length; plain int division loses the fraction.

cards.front_md: What is a square matrix?
cards.back_md: A table with the same number of rows and columns.

cards.front_md: Condition for the left (principal) diagonal
cards.back_md: i == j, or the elements a[i][i].

cards.front_md: Condition for the right diagonal
cards.back_md: i + j == n - 1, or the elements a[i][n - 1 - i].

cards.front_md: Left diagonal sum with one loop
cards.back_md: `ls = ls + a[i][i];` for i from 0 to n - 1.

cards.front_md: Which element is on both diagonals?
cards.back_md: For odd n, the centre a[n / 2][n / 2]; for even n there is none.

cards.front_md: Sum of both diagonals, each element once
cards.back_md: left sum + right sum - centre element (odd n); or one test with i == j || i + j == n - 1.

cards.front_md: Why are diagonals found for square matrices only?
cards.back_md: Rows must equal columns; otherwise a[i][i] can fall outside the columns and cause an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

questions.stem_md: In Java, what is a double-dimensional (two-dimensional) array?

options.text_md: An array that can store only two values
An array whose elements are themselves arrays, so that the data is arranged in rows and columns
An array whose size is doubled every time an element is added
Two single-dimensional arrays declared in the same statement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** An array whose elements are themselves arrays, so that the data is arranged in rows and columns. A double-dimensional array holds a table of values of one data type. Each row is itself a single-dimensional array, and an element is identified by two subscripts, the row and the column. Its size is fixed when it is created, and it is not limited to two values.
